questions.prompt: Which two clauses are required in every SOQL query?
options: SELECT and FROM
SELECT and WHERE
FROM and ORDER BY
WHERE and LIMIT
questions.explain: SELECT and FROM are the only required clauses in a SOQL query; everything else (WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, LIMIT, and more) is optional.
questions.distractorExplain: WHERE is one of the most commonly used clauses, but it's still optional — a query with just SELECT and FROM is perfectly valid and returns every row with no filtering.

questions.prompt: WHERE Name LIKE 'Acme%' would match which of these Account names?
options: Acme Industries
Global Acme Corp
The Acme Company
acme (with a leading space before it)
questions.explain: A trailing % wildcard anchors the match at the start of the string, so only values that begin with 'Acme' match.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: SOQL has no IS NULL syntax. To find Contacts with no Email on file, you write WHERE Email ________ null.
questions.explain: SOQL compares directly against the null keyword using = or != — there is no IS NULL / IS NOT NULL syntax.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about writing a basic SOQL query.
options: SOQL has no SELECT * wildcard — every field must be named explicitly
Fields are returned in the order they're listed in the SELECT clause, not the object's internal field order
A field not named in the SELECT list still returns as null if referenced in Apex
String literals in a WHERE clause must be wrapped in single quotes
LIMIT caps the number of returned rows, applied before ORDER BY sorts them
questions.explain: SOQL has no wildcard and requires an explicit field list, which also controls output order; string literals need single quotes. Referencing an un-queried field throws a runtime error rather than returning null, and LIMIT is applied after sorting, not before.

questions.prompt: Match each date literal to what it represents.
right: Every day within the current calendar month
A relative span covering the last 30 days, evaluated fresh each run
The current year as defined by the org's custom fiscal year configuration
questions.explain: TODAY is a single day, THIS_MONTH spans the current calendar month, LAST_N_DAYS:n is a parameterized relative span, and THIS_FISCAL_YEAR respects a custom fiscal year configuration rather than the calendar year.

questions.prompt: WHERE Industry = 'Technology' OR Industry = 'Finance' AND AnnualRevenue > 1000000, written WITHOUT parentheses, is risky because:
options: AND binds tighter than OR, so it may not group the conditions the way you intended
SOQL requires at least three conditions before AND/OR can be combined
OR cannot be used with AnnualRevenue since it is a numeric field
Industry cannot appear twice in the same WHERE clause
questions.explain: Without explicit parentheses, operator precedence evaluates AND before OR, which can produce a result set different from what was intended.

questions.prompt: Put these SOQL clauses in the order they appear in a query.
questions.explain: A SOQL query's clauses follow this fixed order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, then LIMIT (with OFFSET after LIMIT).

questions.prompt: What is the documented maximum value for OFFSET in a SOQL query, and what happens if you exceed it?
options: 2,000 rows; exceeding it raises a NUMBER_OUTSIDE_VALID_RANGE error
50,000 rows; exceeding it silently truncates the results
100 rows; exceeding it is ignored
There is no maximum for SOQL's OFFSET clause
questions.explain: SOQL's OFFSET is capped at 2,000 rows; going past it raises a NUMBER_OUTSIDE_VALID_RANGE error rather than being silently handled.

questions.prompt: For a custom lookup field with API name Project__c, what relationship name do you use to traverse it in SOQL?
options: Project__r
Project__c
Project_Rel__c
ProjectLookup
questions.explain: Custom relationship traversal replaces the __c suffix with __r — Project__c becomes Project__r when used as a relationship path.
questions.distractorExplain: Project__c is the field's own API name, used for direct DML and field access — but traversing it as a relationship in a SOQL query requires the __r form instead, not the field's own __c name.

questions.prompt: SELECT Name, (SELECT FirstName FROM Contacts) FROM Account returns what shape of result?
options: One row per Account, each carrying a nested list of its related Contact records
One row per Contact, with the Account's Name flattened onto it
A single aggregated row summarizing every Account and Contact
An error, since Contacts must be written as Contact (singular)
questions.explain: A parent-to-child subquery nests the child records' fields under each parent row — the opposite shape of a child-to-parent dot-notation query.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SOQL aggregate functions.
options: COUNT() with empty parentheses counts every matching row, regardless of nulls in any field
COUNT(fieldName) counts only rows where that specific field is non-null
SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX all ignore null values in the field being aggregated
An aggregate query without GROUP BY returns one row per matching record
MIN and MAX can be used on date fields, not just numeric fields
questions.explain: COUNT() counts all rows regardless of nulls, while COUNT(fieldName) and the other aggregates (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) skip nulls in that field. MIN/MAX work on dates too. An aggregate query without GROUP BY collapses to a single summary row, not one row per record.

questions.prompt: If 500 Contacts exist but only 420 have a non-null Email, what does COUNT(Email) return?
questions.explain: COUNT(fieldName) counts only rows where that field is non-null — 420 contacts actually have an email on file.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ filters grouped results after aggregation, while WHERE filters individual rows before grouping happens.
questions.explain: HAVING operates after aggregation on the grouped/aggregate values; WHERE operates before aggregation on individual rows.

questions.prompt: Match each business question shape to the SOQL pattern that best fits it.
left: Accounts that have at least one closed-won Opportunity, no Opportunity fields needed
Each Account together with the full list of its related Contacts
A single Event's What field resolving to either an Account or Opportunity, needing different fields per type
questions.explain: A semi-join filters by a related fact without needing the related object's fields; an anti-join is its negation; a parent-to-child subquery nests the actual related records; TYPEOF branches on a polymorphic field's resolved type to select different fields per type.

questions.prompt: What is the documented limit on subqueries in a single semi-join or anti-join query?
options: At most two subqueries total
Unlimited subqueries
Exactly one subquery
At most five subqueries
questions.explain: SOQL documents a limit of at most two subqueries total in a single semi-join or anti-join query, along with at most two IN/NOT IN statements per WHERE clause.

questions.prompt: Why does SELECT What.Phone FROM Event fail without a TYPEOF clause?
options: SOQL doesn't know in advance which object type's fields it should look up, since What is polymorphic and can resolve to several types
Phone is never a valid field on any object related to Event
Event does not support any relationship queries
What.Phone requires a semi-join to work
questions.explain: Because What can resolve to different object types depending on the record, SOQL can't resolve a plain field reference against it without TYPEOF explicitly branching by type.

questions.prompt: In Apex, how is a SOSL search term written, compared to the Developer Console Query Editor?
options: In single quotes in Apex, versus curly braces in the Query Editor
Identically, in curly braces, in both contexts
In double quotes in Apex, versus parentheses in the Query Editor
SOSL cannot be run from Apex at all
questions.explain: The Query Editor and API use curly braces around the search term; Apex uses single quotes for the same FIND statement.

questions.prompt: Select every valid SOSL IN SearchGroup value.
options: ALL FIELDS
NAME FIELDS
EMAIL FIELDS
AGGREGATE FIELDS
PHONE FIELDS
questions.explain: ALL FIELDS, NAME FIELDS, EMAIL FIELDS, PHONE FIELDS, and SIDEBAR FIELDS are the documented SearchGroup values. AGGREGATE FIELDS is not a real SOSL search group — aggregation is a SOQL concept, not a SOSL one.

questions.prompt: Why is SOSL generally a better fit than a SOQL LIKE '%term%' query for a loose, free-text lookup?
options: A leading-wildcard LIKE can't use an index and scans broadly, while SOSL uses a search index built for this kind of lookup
SOQL's LIKE operator cannot technically match the same records SOSL can find
SOSL has no governor limits at all
LIKE only works on numeric fields
questions.explain: A leading % wildcard prevents index use entirely, forcing a broad scan; SOSL's search index is purpose-built for efficient free-text matching.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a single SOSL search has a shared row budget of ________ records, divided across every object type named in a multi-object RETURNING clause.
questions.explain: SOSL's 2,000-row limit per search is a shared budget across all object types in a multi-object search, not a per-object allowance.

questions.prompt: In Apex, FIND 'Acme' RETURNING Account(Id, Name), Contact(Id, FirstName) returns a List<List<SObject>>. What does searchResults[1] contain?
options: The Contact results
The Account results
A combined list of both objects' results
Nothing — SOSL results in Apex are not indexable
questions.explain: Position in the returned List<List<SObject>> matches the order objects were listed in RETURNING — index 0 is Account, index 1 is Contact.

questions.prompt: A requirement reads: 'find every account with zero opportunities that are Closed Lost.' Which pattern fits this requirement?
options: An anti-join: WHERE Id NOT IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity WHERE StageName = 'Closed Lost')
A semi-join: WHERE Id IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity WHERE StageName = 'Closed Lost')
A parent-to-child subquery nesting all Opportunities under each Account
A SOSL search scoped to NAME FIELDS
questions.explain: 'Zero opportunities matching a condition' is the anti-join pattern — NOT IN with a subquery — the inverse of a semi-join, which would instead find accounts WITH at least one match.

questions.prompt: What does Database.query(queryStr) return in Apex, and why?
options: A generic SObject or List<SObject>, because Apex doesn't know the concrete object type at compile time
Always a specific typed list like List<Account>
An AggregateResult in every case
A QueryLocator, meant for Batch Apex
questions.explain: Since the queried object is only known at runtime in dynamic SOQL, Database.query returns the generic SObject/List<SObject> type rather than a specific sObject type.

questions.prompt: Why does a bind variable (WHERE Industry = :filterValue) prevent SOQL injection, while concatenating the same value into a query string does not?
options: The bind variable's value is always passed as data for comparison, never as text that could be interpreted as query syntax
Bind variables strip all special characters from the input automatically
Bind variables only work with numeric values, so text-based injection becomes impossible
Bind variables disable the WHERE clause entirely, making injection moot
questions.explain: A bind variable passes the value purely as data — it can never break out of its intended context and add new query logic, unlike a value spliced directly into the query string.

questions.prompt: Select every practice that helps SOQL query performance at scale.
options: Querying once outside a loop instead of running a query inside each loop iteration
Selecting only the fields actually needed, instead of a wide field list
Preferring = or IN over != or NOT LIKE where business logic allows
Adding a leading wildcard to every LIKE pattern, e.g. '%term%', for more thorough matches
Explicitly filtering out nulls with != null where it helps the optimizer
questions.explain: Querying outside loops, narrow field lists, selective operators, and explicit null exclusion all help performance. A leading wildcard in LIKE does the opposite — it prevents index use and forces a broader scan.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a standard-indexed filter is considered selective if it matches fewer than ________ percent of the first 1,000,000 targeted records.
questions.explain: The documented standard-index selectivity threshold is under 30% of the first million targeted records (and under 15% beyond that first million).

questions.prompt: In the Query Plan tool, what does a leading operation type of TableScan indicate?
options: The optimizer intends to scan the table broadly rather than use an index
The query is guaranteed to be the fastest possible plan
The query will fail at runtime
The query is an aggregate query
questions.explain: TableScan means the optimizer's plan involves a broad scan instead of an index lookup — generally undesirable for a query expected to perform well at scale.

questions.prompt: Match each governor limit to its documented value, per Apex transaction.
left: Rows retrieved by a single SOSL search
questions.explain: Per transaction: 100 synchronous SOQL queries (200 asynchronous), 50,000 total SOQL rows, 20 SOSL searches, and a 2,000-row cap shared across a single SOSL search's results.

questions.prompt: What happens to a skinny table if you change the data type of a field included in it?
options: The skinny table becomes invalid, and Salesforce Customer Support must create a new one
The skinny table updates itself automatically with no action needed
Nothing changes — skinny tables are unaffected by field type changes
Only the sandbox copy of the skinny table is affected, never production
questions.explain: Altering the type of a field included in a skinny table invalidates it; a new skinny table has to be requested from Salesforce Customer Support.

questions.prompt: Put these large-data-volume escalation steps in the recommended order, from first to last.
items: Write selective filters and query outside of loops
Mark fields External ID/Unique or request a custom index
Request a skinny table from Salesforce Customer Support
Use PK chunking via the Bulk API for very large batch processing
questions.explain: Standard coding best practices (selective filters, bulkified queries) come first, then custom indexing, with skinny tables reserved as a last resort after those are exhausted; PK chunking is the separate, documented answer for walking very large objects in Bulk API batches rather than relying on OFFSET.
